entry.title: Napoleon's First Masterpiece: 6 Victories in 15 Days | Italy 1796

media:group.media:title: Napoleon's First Masterpiece: 6 Victories in 15 Days | Italy 1796
media:group.media:description:
The Italian campaign of 1796: Napoleon's first command of an army, and the first time he used the method that made him. In March 1796 the Directory gave its smallest, hungriest army to a general of twenty-six. One of his battalions had just refused to march: it had no shoes and no pay. Facing him stood two armies, Austrian and Piedmontese, some fifty thousand men.
He drove into the join between them. Montenotte, Millesimo, Dego, Mondovì: in two weeks the allies were torn apart and the Kingdom of Sardinia was out of the war. "Soldiers," he told his army at Cherasco, "in fifteen days you have won six victories." The figures were his own, and he was generous with them. Then he crossed the Po where nobody expected him, stormed the bridge of Lodi, and rode into Milan.
This animated battle-map documentary follows the campaign day by day, on the real terrain of the Ligurian Apennines and the Lombard plain: the redoubt on Monte Negino, the castle of Cosseria, Dego lost and retaken, the armistice with its false clause, the death of Laharpe, and the two hundred metres of wooden bridge over the Adda. It also follows the money: twenty million francs from Lombardy, and the art that went to Paris.
CHAPTERS 00:00 Lodi, 10 May 1796 01:03 Europe in 1796: France against the Coalition 04:17 A general of twenty-six takes command 05:16 The Austrians strike first: Monte Negino 06:16 Montenotte: the first victory 07:16 Millesimo and the castle of Cosseria 08:33 Dego, taken, lost and retaken 09:57 Turning on Piedmont: Ceva, San Michele, Mondovì 11:37 Cherasco: "In fifteen days you have won six victories" 13:12 Crossing the Po at Piacenza 14:21 The race to the Adda 15:15 The bridge of Lodi 16:55 Milan, and the bill 18:10 "The first spark of my ambition"
Eighteen years later, with all of Europe closing in on Paris, he reached for the same method again: Napoleon's Last Masterpiece, the Six Days' Campaign of 1814, is already on the channel.

entry.title: The Battle Napoleon Couldn’t Afford to Win | Borodino 1812

media:group.media:title: The Battle Napoleon Couldn’t Afford to Win | Borodino 1812
media:group.media:description:
The Battle of Borodino, 7 September 1812: the bloodiest day of the Napoleonic Wars. Seventy miles from Moscow, Napoleon finally got the great battle he had chased across Russia. More than 70,000 men fell in a single day. And his best troops, almost 20,000 men of the Imperial Guard, never went in.
All day his marshals begged him to send in the Guard and finish it. All day he refused. "And if there is another battle tomorrow," he said, "what shall I fight it with?" This animated battle-map documentary follows the day hour by hour: the flèches, where Bagration fell; the Poles at Utitsa; the cavalry raid that cost the French an hour, perhaps two; the Great Redoubt, stormed from the front while cuirassiers rode into its open rear; and some 1,200 guns on one field.
When night fell, the Russians were still there. Both sides claimed the victory. A week later Napoleon was in Moscow, and Moscow was burning.
CHAPTERS 00:00 Napoleon's last card: the Imperial Guard 00:45 The invasion of Russia 02:35 The position at Borodino 04:07 Shevardino and the eve of battle 05:47 Dawn: "the sun of Austerlitz" 06:54 The flèches: Davout, Ney and Bagration 08:29 Utitsa: the Poles on the old Smolensk road 09:06 "Send in the Guard" 10:52 The Great Redoubt 13:08 Night: 70,000 men in one day 14:59 Both sides claim victory 16:08 Moscow burns 17:18 The road home

entry.title: Napoleon's Last Masterpiece: 4 Battles in 5 Days | France 1814

media:group.media:title: Napoleon's Last Masterpiece: 4 Battles in 5 Days | France 1814
media:group.media:description:
The Six Days Campaign, February 1814: Napoleon's last masterpiece. France was invaded, 200,000 allied soldiers were marching on Paris, and Napoleon had 70,000. Then, in five days, he fought four battles and won them all: Champaubert, Montmirail, Château-Thierry and Vauchamps.
One night at Nogent, one of his ministers found him lying on the floor among his maps and pins. "At this moment," Napoleon said, "I am beating Blücher with my eye." This animated battle-map documentary follows how he did it. Blücher's Army of Silesia was strung out along the Marne like a snake. Napoleon dragged his guns through the mud of the Saint-Gond marshes and struck it in the middle, then turned on each piece in turn. In five days the Army of Silesia lost some 16,000 men out of about 56,000. Napoleon lost about 4,000.
It was not enough. Seven weeks later, the marshal who helped him win it went over to the enemy.

entry.title: Berezina 1812 - The River That Became Napoleon's Worst Nightmare

media:group.media:title: Berezina 1812 - The River That Became Napoleon's Worst Nightmare
media:group.media:description:
Berezina 1812 follows Napoleon's retreat from Russia through animated battle maps, 3D terrain and the decisions that kept an escape route open.
From the crossing of the Niemen and the burning of Moscow to the trap at the Berezina, watch the Grande Armee shrink across the campaign map. Then follow the deception that pulled Chichagov south, General Eble's bridge builders at Studianka, and the fighting on both banks that protected the crossing.
The escape saved Napoleon. It did not undo the catastrophe of the Russian campaign.

entry.title: Did Napoleon Win the Wrong Battle? | Jena-Auerstedt Explained

media:group.media:title: Did Napoleon Win the Wrong Battle? | Jena-Auerstedt Explained
media:group.media:description:
Napoleon won at Jena. But the main Prussian army was somewhere else — facing Davout and a single French corps.
Explore Jena–Auerstedt, 14 October 1806, through animated battle maps and 3D terrain. While Napoleon fought Hohenlohe at Jena, Davout's roughly 27,000 men confronted a Prussian main army of around 60,000 at Auerstedt.
How did Napoleon misread the enemy's position? Why did Blücher's cavalry fail against French squares? And how did Davout turn an outnumbered defence into a victory?
Follow the campaign from Prussia's ultimatum and the march through Thuringia to the fog at Hassenhausen, Rüchel's late arrival, Bernadotte's absence from the decisive fighting, and the collapse that opened the road to Berlin.
CHAPTERS 00:00 Napoleon won the wrong battle 00:27 Prussia challenges Napoleon 01:51 The invasion through Thuringia 02:55 The army Napoleon missed 03:51 Night on the Landgrafenberg 04:48 Jena: the battle in the fog 05:57 Auerstedt: Davout meets the main army 07:01 Brunswick falls and command breaks down 08:04 The Prussian collapse at Jena 08:50 Davout strikes back 09:38 Napoleon learns the truth 10:34 The collapse of Prussia and the road east

entry.title: Austerlitz 1805: How Napoleon Trapped a Larger Army

media:group.media:title: Austerlitz 1805: How Napoleon Trapped a Larger Army
media:group.media:description:
Austerlitz 1805: how Napoleon trapped a larger army at the Battle of Austerlitz. Explore the terrain, troop movements, and decisive maneuvers through animated battle maps.
Napoleon gave away the high ground and made his army look ready to retreat. That apparent weakness helped draw the Allied army into his trap.
Follow the Battle of Austerlitz on animated tactical maps: the approach to Moravia, the struggle for Telnitz and Sokolnitz, Soult's attack on the Pratzen Heights, and the collapse of the Allied left.
On 2 December 1805, Napoleon faced the armies of Russia and Austria in the Battle of the Three Emperors. Why did the Allies leave the heights? How did Davout's exhausted troops keep the French right from breaking? And when did an apparent Allied advantage become a disaster?
The film also follows the 1805 campaign through Ulm, Trafalgar and Vienna, then separates the famous frozen-pond story from its exaggerated legend.
